task: Finalize this conceptual documentation draft for analysts who build weekly reports in Linden Catalog 1.3. Explain how published snapshots and report bindings determine the data a report run reads. Keep the scope on the reader's mental model and the worked reporting examples.
source_facts: Linden Catalog 1.3 is a synthetic reporting product. This specification is authoritative for every product behavior and example in this document. A collection is a named dataset whose working rows editors can change. A snapshot is the complete, immutable set of rows captured by a successful publication of one collection; it is not a change log, a sample, or a live view. A snapshot identifier is unique only within its collection. Publishing creates a new snapshot without changing existing snapshots and moves that collection's latest alias to the new snapshot. latest is a movable alias, not an identifier of an immutable snapshot. Saving working-row edits without publishing does not change latest. A report binding selects a collection and either a specific snapshot identifier (a pinned binding) or latest (a tracking binding). A pinned binding continues to select its specified snapshot after later publications. A tracking binding resolves latest when a run starts. The resolved snapshot is fixed for that entire run, even if publication occurs during execution. Every completed run records the resolved collection name and snapshot identifier in Run details; these two values identify its data input. For a single-collection report, rerunning the same report definition and parameters against that same snapshot gives the same input rows. A snapshot does not freeze a report's formulas, parameters, or presentation, and this guarantee is about input rows rather than identical rendered results. Separate collections publish independently. A report using multiple collections resolves each binding at its own run start, but there is no transactionally consistent cross-collection snapshot: selected snapshots can represent different publication times. Analysts needing an aligned comparison must choose snapshots known to represent the same reporting cutoff and pin each collection explicitly. Collections and snapshots use the same current access policy: permission to read the collection is required at run time. Pinning does not preserve permissions. If permission is removed before a later run, that run cannot read the snapshot. Existing snapshots are retained until the collection is deleted; publication does not evict earlier snapshots. Deleting a collection deletes its snapshots. If a pinned snapshot is unavailable, the run fails with snapshot_unavailable and does not substitute latest. Snapshot identifiers should therefore be recorded together with collection names. In the single-collection example, the orders collection has snapshot s17 with 240 rows. An editor saves 12 additional working rows without publishing; s17 and latest still select 240 rows. A subsequent publication creates s18 with 252 rows and moves latest to s18. A report pinned to orders/s17 still reads 240 rows. A tracking run started before publication reads s17 throughout, while a new tracking run afterward reads s18. Pinning a comparison report to orders/s17 and a second comparison report to orders/s18 separates the before and after inputs; neither snapshot records which twelve rows were added, so the report must compare the row sets. A wrong value in an approved snapshot cannot be repaired by editing the working collection alone: corrected rows must be published as a new snapshot. Analysts can explicitly change a report's pinned binding to another existing snapshot. For an approved reporting period, repin to the corrected snapshot when the revised input is approved. The original snapshot remains unchanged and available while its collection exists, allowing comparison of the original and corrected inputs. In the multi-collection example, orders/s18 and refunds/r6 are the approved Friday-cutoff snapshots. A later corrections publication creates orders/s19 on Monday while refunds latest still names r6. Tracking both collections can therefore mix Monday orders with Friday refunds. Pinning orders/s18 and refunds/r6 is the approved Friday comparison. Choosing a pinned binding is recommended for approved reporting periods; choosing tracking is recommended for a monitoring report that intentionally follows each new publication. Support investigations should capture collection, resolved snapshot, report definition version, and parameters from the relevant run. The page is conceptual guidance for weekly-report analysts, not a publication or administration procedure.

# How snapshot bindings shape a report

This explanation is for analysts building weekly reports in Linden Catalog 1.3. It describes which rows a report reads and how to make that choice deliberate. Publication and collection administration are separate workflows; here, the useful starting point is the relationship between a collection, its snapshots, and a report binding.

## Summary

Use a pinned binding for an approved reporting period. Use a tracking binding when a monitoring report should follow new publications. Either choice selects one fixed snapshot for a run: a publication during execution does not change the rows that run reads. For an investigation, start with the collection and resolved snapshot recorded in Run details.

## Three objects with different jobs

A **collection** is a named dataset with working rows that editors can change. A **snapshot** is the complete, immutable set of rows captured by a successful publication of that collection. It is neither a sample nor a log of changes. Editing the working rows does not edit any previously published snapshot.

The name **latest** is a movable alias for the collection's most recently published snapshot. Publishing creates a new snapshot and moves that alias. Saving edits without publishing leaves the alias where it was. This distinction matters when someone says the data was updated: a saved edit and a publication have different consequences for report readers.

A **binding** is the report's selection of a collection and a snapshot. A pinned binding names a specific snapshot identifier. A tracking binding names latest, which is resolved when the run starts. Snapshot identifiers are unique only within a collection, so record the collection name alongside the identifier rather than treating an identifier as a catalog-wide address.

## Follow one collection through a publication

Suppose the orders collection has snapshot s17 with 240 rows. An editor adds and saves twelve working rows. Until those edits are published, both s17 and latest still select the original 240 rows. A report cannot see the saved additions merely by switching from a pinned binding to a tracking binding.

The editor then publishes s18 with 252 rows. The latest alias now names s18, while s17 remains a 240-row snapshot. The outcomes depend on the binding and the run's start:

| Report choice | Input rows |
| --- | --- |
| Pinned to orders/s17 | 240 rows from s17 |
| Tracking run started before publication | 240 rows from s17 |
| Tracking run started after publication | 252 rows from s18 |

The middle row is important for a report that takes time to finish. A tracking binding is resolved once at run start, not repeatedly while rows are processed. The running report continues reading s17 even after latest moves. A later tracking run selects s18; it does not retroactively change the earlier run's input.

For a before-and-after comparison, pin one comparison report to orders/s17 and another to orders/s18. Each snapshot contains a full row set. Neither is a record of the twelve additions, so identifying those additions requires comparing the row sets rather than interpreting s18 as an incremental change file.

### Correcting an approved input

If an approved snapshot contains a wrong value, editing that value in the working collection does not repair the approved snapshot. Publish the corrected rows as a new snapshot, then explicitly change the report's pin when the revised input is approved. Keeping the original snapshot available lets a reviewer distinguish the original input from the correction; it does not make the original value correct.

## What a pin makes repeatable

For a single-collection report, the same report definition and parameters against the same snapshot read the same input rows. That is the useful boundary of the snapshot guarantee. A snapshot does not freeze formulas, parameter choices, or presentation, so the snapshot identifier alone is not a promise of identical rendered results.

Every completed run records its resolved collection and snapshot in Run details. When investigating a difference, capture those values together with the report definition version and parameters. This gives the investigation both the data selection and the report context, instead of assuming that two runs using the word latest necessarily read the same rows.

## Combining collections requires another decision

Collections publish independently. A report resolves each collection binding when its run starts, but there is no transactionally consistent snapshot across collections. Selecting latest for every binding can therefore combine data from different publication times. Starting all those selections in one report does not establish a shared reporting cutoff.

For example, orders/s18 and refunds/r6 are the approved Friday-cutoff inputs. On Monday, an orders correction is published as s19, while refunds latest still names r6. A tracking report can now combine Monday orders with Friday refunds. For the approved Friday comparison, explicitly pin orders/s18 and refunds/r6. Choose snapshots known to represent the same cutoff rather than relying on their positions behind the latest aliases.

## Availability and access are separate from immutability

Publishing a newer snapshot does not evict older ones. Existing snapshots remain until their collection is deleted; deleting the collection also deletes its snapshots. Immutability describes the snapshot's rows while it exists, not an independent lifetime beyond the collection that owns it.

A pinned binding also does not preserve access rights. Reading any snapshot requires permission to read its collection at run time. If that permission is removed before a later run, the later run cannot read the snapshot, even though its binding still names the same input.

If a pinned snapshot is unavailable, the run fails with snapshot_unavailable. It does not substitute latest. Treat that failure as an unavailable selected input, rather than evidence that a newer publication has silently changed the approved report's rows.
